summary: A 1977 note describing a time server, a service that provides the current time to other hosts on the network. Its status is unknown.

plainLanguage.summary: One computer in the group answers the question what time is it, so all the others can set their clocks.

questions: how did early hosts get network time
how do networked computers synchronize time
what is the time server protocol
why did early networks need time servers
subtitle: A simple protocol for hosts to synchronize their clocks over the network

tldr.problem: Not all ARPANET hosts had accurate clocks, and human or machine errors made time synchronization unreliable. Hosts needed a quick way to check and correct their system time.
tldr.mechanism: A Time Server listens on socket 37 and returns the current time as a 32-bit binary number representing seconds since midnight 1 January 1900 GMT. The server closes the connection after sending the time.
tldr.outcome: Any host can poll one or more independent time servers to quickly confirm or correct its notion of the current time.

today: RFC 738 is an early time synchronization protocol and is not in use on the modern Internet. The Network Time Protocol (RFC 5905) superseded it with a more sophisticated algorithm that handles network latency and clock drift. However, the simplicity of RFC 738's design influenced later standards.

sections.title: The Need for Network Time
sections.content:
RFC 738 describes a Time Server protocol developed at MIT. The service is straightforward: it lets any host ask several independent time servers for the current time and use those answers to correct its own system clock.

Because not all systems had an onboard clock and because human error in setting time was common, the ARPANET needed a simple, reliable way to distribute authoritative time across the network. The Time Server protocol meets this need with minimal overhead.
sections.plainLanguage: Some computers on the network didn't know what time it was. A Time Server lets other computers phone home and ask, "What time is it right now?"

sections.title: How the Protocol Works
sections.content:
A Time Server listens on socket 37 (octal 45). A client connects to that socket; the server does not follow the usual ICP (Initial Connection Protocol) sequence. Instead, immediately upon connection, the server sends a 32-bit binary time value and closes the connection. If the server cannot determine its own time, it refuses the connection or closes without sending data.

This is intentionally simple: no handshakes, no options, no negotiation. A client simply connects, reads the time, and disconnects.
sections.plainLanguage: You knock on the door, someone hands you a number that tells you what time it is, and closes the door. That's it.

sections.title: Time Format
sections.content:
The time is encoded as the number of seconds since 0000 (midnight) on 1 January 1900 GMT. This epoch covers the time range until the year 2036 without overflow in a 32-bit unsigned integer. For example, the most recent leap year as of the RFC's writing began at timestamp 2,398,291,200, corresponding to 0000 on 1 January 1976 GMT.

This fixed epoch is unusual by modern standards but was practical for the 1970s. The reference point of 1900 is historical; it was chosen simply as a round date far enough in the past.
sections.plainLanguage: The server sends a big number: how many seconds have ticked since midnight on January 1, 1900. It's a simple way to represent any time without worrying about calendars.

sections.title: Practical Use
sections.content:
A host that doubts its clock can poll several independent Time Servers and use the median or mean response to set its system time with high confidence. The protocol's simplicity and statelessness make it resilient: the server never forgets anything, and clients do not need to maintain connection state.

The RFC implies that using multiple servers is important: polling several independent sites on the network makes it possible to quickly confirm or correct a system's idea of the time and spot anomalies when one server gives an outlier.
sections.plainLanguage: If you ask a few different people what time it is, you can trust the answer better. You just keep calling until enough servers agree.
